posts.text:
Why Democrats are furious that Jensen Huang is back.

Read Hakeem Jeffries' statement carefully. It opens with Jensen. It closes with "ironclad export control legislation" in the NDAA. That's not an accident. That's the tell.

The scandal was never the point. The leverage was.

There are now two camps in AI.

The open camp: build, ship, compete, let a thousand models run on millions of machines.

The regulators: licenses, committees, moratoriums, export regimes. Democrats, Brussels, Bill Gates, the supranational agencies. They all talk about "regulating AI" for one simple reason. They've understood something.

If superintelligence is open, their entire model collapses. The foundations that fund the think tanks, that fund the universities, that manufacture the narrative, that justifies the agenda. An open AI audits all of it in thirty seconds. You can't rule through narrative when anyone can check the numbers.

So it can't be open. They need a toll booth.

Jensen was a problem for them. He sells the shovels, and he refuses to wall off the world. He's on the same line as Elon and most serious builders: AI should serve humanity, not a caste that captured every institution.

For eleven days, they had him out. A scandal, a resignation, a board swearing he'd never return, a headhunter already hired. The people who want compute under lock and key finally had their story.

Today he's back. Unanimous board vote. And within hours, the incoming Speaker is promising a "wide-ranging investigation" and new export laws.

They're screaming because they know what's at stake. This isn't a policy debate. It's a fight to the death.

On one side:
The Democrats.
The globalist bloc.
The supranational machine: the UN, the WHO, Brussels.

On the other:
Free, sovereign nations that want to work together.
That want to compete, fiercely and fairly.

That refuse to be managed by an elite nobody elected.

And let's name the industry's most effective lobbyist for the first camp: Anthropic. Years pushing export controls. Their CEO compared selling Nvidia chips to China to selling nuclear weapons to North Korea. 

Jensen summed them up perfectly: they think AI is so dangerous that only they should be allowed to build it.

Anthropic went public last week. I hope their stock ends up exactly where their vision of the future belongs.

posts.text:
At 1:20 a.m., the shelter director checked the camera feed from home and saw the dog everyone was afraid to approach take a step toward a man.

The man sat on a blanket with a paperback open in his lap. He kept his head down as the dog came close enough to rest his chin on one of his boots. A few moments later, he closed the book and wiped his eyes on his sleeve.

For the first time in years, the dog had reached out to a person on his own.

Nobody asked to meet the dog in Kennel 32.

You could hear the shelter dogs from halfway down the hall. Some barked at the sight of a leash. Others heard footsteps and called out for a treat or a little attention. Visitors usually smiled as they went from gate to gate.

When they reached Kennel 32, their smiles faded.

Inside sat Boone, a ninety-pound charcoal-gray Cane Corso. His chest seemed to take up half the kennel. A notch split one ear, old scars ran across his neck and shoulders, and a rough patch of skin covered part of his muzzle.

He sat against the rear wall and followed people with his pale eyes. He rarely blinked. People who might have understood a bark or a growl didn’t know what to make of a dog who could sit that still.

A sign on the gate warned visitors to keep out unless a staff member was with them. Another said Boone still needed a behavioral assessment. Plenty of people turned away after reading the signs. The rest took one look at his size and scars and usually did the same.

His records filled a binder. Two returns, an uncertain history, suspected mistreatment, and restrictions on who could handle him. Each time Boone moved to another shelter, the binder got thicker.

The people who worked around him every day saw what frightened him. If a gate banged shut, he threw himself into a corner. A dropped food bowl could leave him shaking. Sometimes a man yelling elsewhere in the building was enough to send him flat to the concrete, where he’d stay for hours.

A visitor might spend ten seconds in front of his kennel and walk away thinking Boone was dangerous. The staff had spent enough time with him to see how much of each day he spent bracing for something to happen.

Three shelters had tried to help him. Nobody had found a way to get close enough for Boone to feel comfortable. The county scheduled one last behavioral review, and the staff knew how few options they had left.

That was when Daniel showed up.

He was a quiet man in his late forties, wearing faded jeans and old hiking boots. He had no professional training in animal behavior. He’d brought a paperback mystery.

At the kennel, the director warned him that Boone’s reactions could be hard to predict. As she spoke, Boone pressed himself farther into the corner. His legs stiffened, and his breath came fast and shallow.

Daniel watched him for a moment.

“How long do you think he’s felt this way?” he asked.

The director said she didn’t know what had happened before he came to the shelter.

Daniel nodded. “I think he remembers.”

He asked for a blanket. Then he went inside, shut the gate, and spread the blanket on the concrete. He sat down, opened his book, and started to read.

A few volunteers protested. They wanted to know what he’d do if Boone rushed him. Daniel looked up long enough to say he didn’t think Boone would.

Five minutes went by. Then fifteen. After half an hour, Daniel was still reading, and Boone was still in his corner. Daniel never looked directly at him or stretched out a hand.

Staff gathered at the window. One volunteer asked what Daniel was doing. The director watched him turn a page and said she figured he was just keeping Boone company.

The lights dimmed as the shelter closed. Staff went home, and the security cameras kept recording. Daniel stayed on the floor with his book.

A little before midnight, Boone took a step. He took one more, then stopped, trembling from his shoulders down. 👇

posts.text:
NIGERIANS, GO AND VERIFY (8)

TRANSFORMING COMMERCE, INDUSTRY AND INFRASTRUCTURE: BUILDING AN ECONOMY THAT WORKS 

Peter Obi

I have always believed that economic development must go beyond the construction of roads and buildings. It must create opportunities, stimulate enterprise, support local industries, and improve the productive capacity of society. Government must not merely spend money; it must create the conditions that enable people and businesses to prosper.

When I assumed office in 2006, Anambra State already possessed enormous entrepreneurial energy. From Onitsha to Nnewi, Awka, and other commercial centres, our people had demonstrated remarkable ingenuity and enterprise. What was required was a government that could provide the infrastructure, institutional support, and enabling environment to harness this potential.

Under the Anambra Integrated Development Strategy (ANIDS), we therefore pursued a deliberate programme of commercial and industrial development, with particular emphasis on public-private partnerships (PPPs). Our objective was to modernise the business environment, attract investment, strengthen indigenous enterprises, and create employment.

Our approach was guided by a simple conviction: commerce must be supported by production, and industrial development must be supported by infrastructure. We could not continue to depend largely on buying and selling without deliberately creating the conditions for manufacturing, processing, and value addition.

MODERNISING COMMERCE: THE ONITSHA BUSINESS PARKS
Recognising Onitsha’s historical position as the commercial hub of the South-East, we initiated the First and Second Onitsha Business Parks. We wanted to provide organised, modern, and secure business environments capable of accommodating growing corporate and financial activities.

The parks attracted important financial institutions and corporate operations, including facilities for banks, alongside capital market operators and other businesses.

We also conceived the second phase of the Onitsha Business Village as a centre for information and communications technology-related activities. The intention was to move beyond traditional commercial arrangements and provide facilities that would accommodate emerging business opportunities and technology-driven enterprises.

Another initiative was the LG World-ANIDS project, conceived as a one-stop centre for electronic goods, services, and training. We wanted to connect commerce with technology, skills development, and modern business practices.

Our intention was to move commercial activities beyond the limitations of informal arrangements and provide the infrastructure necessary for modern corporate operations.

DEVELOPING HOSPITALITY AND TOURISM: AGULU LAKE RESORT AND PROTEA HOTEL 
We also recognised that a growing commercial centre must have the hospitality infrastructure to support investors, business travellers, and tourists. A state that seeks to attract investment must be prepared to accommodate those who come to do business. This informed our conception of two important projects.

The Agulu Lake Resort was designed to harness the natural beauty and tourism potential of Agulu Lake, creating a destination for leisure, hospitality, and conferences. Beyond tourism, we saw the project as an opportunity to stimulate economic activities in the surrounding communities and create employment.

Similarly, the five-star Protea Hotel project in the GRA, Onitsha, was conceived as a public-private partnership to provide high-standard accommodation and hospitality services. We envisaged a facility that would serve investors, business travellers, and visitors while expanding the State’s hospitality infrastructure. Although the project was subsequently abandoned, its original conception reflected our determination to provide the facilities required by a modern commercial economy.
